essential: Carter's refusal to help, and Tuppence's realization that without Tommy she is 'a rudderless ship'. Include her self-scolding about being sentimental.
No sign of Boris. Tuppence persuades a reluctant Julius ('It can do no harm') to visit Sir James on her Sunday afternoon out.
Sir James's library has one wall of works on crime. He admits his earlier remark was a hint, and he gives the 'without prejudice' young-sister warning.
Tuppence tells Sir James the whole story, including Tommy. Sir James says he has theories about Jane Finn, criticizes Carter, and decides to stay rather than go fishing.
Sir James proposes making Mrs. Vandemeyer talk, keeping bribery in reserve. Julius offers one million dollars, Sir James converts it to over £250,000, and Sir James flushes at the mention of a fee.

The plan: Tuppence returns at nine-thirty, Sir James calls at ten, and Julius waits with the car. Include Sir James's advice to have a good dinner and not think ahead. Keep Tuppence's 'Isn't he a duck?' and Julius's grudging concession.

Tuppence walks in the park, then is drawn back to South Audley Mansions. Albert reports that Rita is packing and has sent for a taxi. Tuppence sends him to telephone Julius, or failing that Sir James.
Tuppence's toothache excuse; the cook has been sent out; the revolver at her temple; the disordered, half-packed bedroom.
Rita demands she drink the sleeping draught. Include the 'poison?'/'Perhaps' exchange and Rita's argument that she does not want a murder hue and cry.
Tuppence stages a grovelling collapse to gain time and get closer. She extracts the oath, throws the glass in Rita's face, and seizes the revolver. Include Rita's 'I have a long memory' threat.

The bribe: Tuppence recalls Boris's 'sell--us' remark and Whittington's 'Rita?'. She offers £100,000 (not the whole million) from an American millionaire friend. Rita can find out where Jane is and will ask Boris about Tommy.

'Who is Mr. Brown?': Rita pales, admits she knows ('I was beautiful... Not beautiful enough'), and demands an oath of secrecy and the money without delay. She then fears listeners ('walls might have ears'), shrieks, points over Tuppence's head, and faints.

voice_profile: Brisk, comic thriller narration in third person, staying mostly close to Tuppence's mind. Her self-mockery ('Little fool') and her money creed are played for comedy but also expose real feeling. The prose is mostly fast dialogue in distinct voices: Julius's American slang ('Sure thing', 'Put me wise', 'Bully'); Sir James's dry, smooth legal phrasing and chin-stroking; Mrs. Vandemeyer's steely melodrama; Albert's cinema-fed Cockney. Short narrative paragraphs carry the sudden reversals. Chapters end on hooks such as 'Now-- _it was empty_.' Emphasis is marked with italics. Double hyphens and broken-off speeches ('----') convey interruption and dread.
